column5: Session cookie replay — attacker reuses stolen cookie to place orders as a real user
column7: Session hijacking is a known technique but requires first obtaining a valid cookie via XSS or device access — not a zero-click attack
column9: Attacker impersonates one specific user; financial and reputational harm per account but contained blast radius
column11: Fix: bind sessions to device fingerprint; short-lived signed tokens

column5: Order repudiation — user claims never placed order to trigger chargeback; no signed audit trail
column7: Active repudiation attacks are rare; chargebacks do occur but are typically individual not coordinated
column9: Financial loss per chargeback; legal risk; no data breach; limited to disputes on individual orders
column11: Fix: log signed client IP + timestamp on every order event

column5: LB strips X-Forwarded-For — all downstream per-IP rate-limiting and forensic attribution silently fail
column7: Requires an LB misconfiguration (operator error) not an external exploit; no credentials or remote access needed
column9: Defeats ALL per-IP security controls simultaneously — rate limiting, blocking, audit — across 100% of traffic
column11: Fix: assert header-forwarding in LB config; alert on its absence at boot

column5: Slowloris — attacker holds 50k connections with slow bodies; LB connection pool exhausted
column7: Publicly available tooling (slowhttptest); no credentials needed; detectable but not blocked by default LB config
column9: Full service outage for all users; SLO breach — 43.8-minute monthly error budget exhausted in one attack
column11: Fix: per-connection read timeout ≤10 s; max concurrent connections per source IP

column5: Non-expiring service-account token used to call /cart/summarise after DIAL_API_KEY leak was never rotated
column7: Requires attacker to have already obtained the token via the prior leak — secondary post-breach threat
column9: Attacker impersonates an internal service; gains access to cart-api endpoints at service tier
column11: Fix: rotate all service-account tokens; enforce 24-hour TTL

column5: Redis cart-state injection — attacker writes tampered payload (negative amounts / discount codes) direct to cache
column7: Requires network access to the Redis port or prior Redis credential; Redis should be internal-only
column9: Fraudulent checkouts processed at scale for all affected sessions; financial impact plus SOC fraud investigation
column11: Fix: authenticate Redis connections; re-validate cart state from Postgres at checkout before committing

column5: DIAL_API_KEY emitted in pod logs at DEBUG level — confirmed plaintext in failure-A describe output
column7: Confirmed happening today: env vars visible in kubectl describe; if DEBUG logging active, also in observability logs; requires only observability read access (developer tier)
column9: Live credential exposure: any developer reads DIAL_API_KEY and DATABASE_URL; unlimited DIAL spend up to $16k cap; DATABASE_URL enables full Postgres dump; cart PII exfiltration via crafted prompts
column11: BLAST RADIUS: DIAL_API_KEY — $16,000 cap breach in <1 hour of automated calls; ~3M customer cart sessions per month exposed via prompt injection; DATABASE_URL — full Postgres dump of all orders and user PII for all customers served by this instance; at ~4,000 summarise calls/hour the key was exposed to any of ~20 developers with observability read access. FIX FIRST: rotate DIAL_API_KEY immediately; rotate DATABASE_URL password; disable DEBUG env-var logging; use secretKeyRef (8.W.2 fix)

column5: Unauthenticated summarise flood — no per-IP rate limit; 1k req/s fans out to DIAL calls exhausting $16k cap
column7: No application-layer rate limit confirmed; any internet user can call the endpoint; no tooling beyond curl needed
column9: $16,000/month DIAL cap exhausted potentially in hours; HTTP 429 returned to all users; full AI feature outage
column11: Fix: per-IP and per-session rate limit at cart-api (≤10 summarise/min per session); DIAL alert at $12k fires before cap

column5: Default service account has get/list/watch on all Secrets — compromised pod reads sibling-service credentials
column7: Requires cart-api to be compromised first (e.g. via T-07 or T-13); exploitation after that is a single API call
column9: Full namespace secret dump: credentials for payment-api and order-api; complete lateral movement
column11: Fix: bind cart-api to a dedicated service account with minimal RBAC (Secrets access only to cart-api-secrets)

column5: Cart item names and prices leave TB2 in every summarise request body — no DPA Article 28 processor agreement confirmed
column7: Happening by design on every call (~3M/month); no exploit needed — structural disclosure at TB2 crossing
column9: GDPR breach risk if provider retains prompts; regulatory fine up to 4% of annual turnover; individual customer PII (items, prices) exposed per call
column11: Fix: confirm DPA with DIAL provider; consider hashing or truncating item names before sending; data minimisation

column5: Prompt injection — user sets cart item name to instruction text; DIAL passes it unsanitised to LLM
column7: Cart item name is free-text user input; no sanitisation layer mentioned; prompt injection scanners and payloads are publicly documented (PromptInject, OWASP LLM Top 10 #1)
column9: Attacker extracts system prompt; manipulates summary output; may pivot to extract other users' context if session isolation is weak in the gateway
column11: Fix: sanitise item names before embedding in prompt; use structured prompt templates with delimiters; log all injected-looking inputs

column5: etcd encryption at rest not confirmed — cart-api-secrets stored as base64 if unencrypted
column7: Requires cluster-admin or direct etcd access; high barrier for external attacker; more of an insider/misconfiguration risk
column9: Complete credential dump: DATABASE_URL + DIAL_API_KEY; same impact as T-07 but via infrastructure path rather than application logs
column11: Fix: enable etcd encryption at rest; confirm with ops team; audit who has cluster-admin

column5: SQL injection via order_id path param — unsanitised concatenation returns all customers' order rows
column7: Path parameter injection is a top OWASP finding; automated scanners (sqlmap) detect it without credentials; public endpoint assumed
column9: Full Postgres dump of all orders and user PII across all customers; GDPR-notifiable breach; regulatory fine; reputational damage
column11: Blast radius: all order records and user PII for every customer in the database. Fix: parameterise the query using prepared statements; add integration test asserting the WHERE clause is user-scoped

column5: Direct DB write via leaked DATABASE_URL bypasses application audit log on order status transitions
column7: Requires DATABASE_URL credential (leaked in first-draft manifest / failure-A pod env); insider or post-breach scenario
column9: Financial fraud (e.g. status set to refunded); audit integrity compromised; forensic gap; limited to what raw SQL can change
column11: Fix: rotate DATABASE_URL password; restrict Postgres user to application-only permissions; row-level audit trigger
